sections.title: Where you are right now
sections.body: You’re dealing with confirmed substance use, not just a hunch, and you suspect it’s happening at least weekly. Your child spends most free time in places and with peers where you expect drugs or alcohol to be around, and you rarely know where your child is. When you try to set limits, it blows up into yelling and slammed doors, so you’ve started dreading any real conversation and often avoid it. Rules are mostly not enforced, your child denies responsibility and blames others, and you’re constantly unsure if you are being too harsh or too soft. Mood and behaviour swing sharply, and your child shuts down when anything emotional comes up. You are worried about safety to the point that sleep and work are affected. You feel alone, with no real support from school or professionals, and the near-daily exhaustion you described makes every step feel heavier. Right now there is no clear plan, just fear and guesswork.

sections.title: Your first three priorities
items: First, steady yourself before doing anything with your child. You’re running on empty, losing sleep, and dreading conflict, which means fear and fatigue are driving a lot of your reactions. For the next few days, your job is to slow your responses down: short pauses before speaking, stepping out of the room when voices rise, and writing down what you want to say instead of saying it in the moment. No new rules, no big talks yet. Your goal is to be calmer and more predictable than the near-daily chaos you see from your child.

Second, get the adults on the same page before you move toward your child. If there is a co-parent, co-guardian, or another parent or guardian on the family side, schedule a specific time within the next 48 hours to agree on a few key rules, rewards, and consequences that you will both actually hold. If contact is strained or distant, your task is still to decide what you will do and communicate it clearly if possible: “Here’s what I’m putting in place and what will happen if use continues.” Alignment on rules, rewards, and consequences has to come before the conversation with your child.

Third, stop doing this completely alone. Reach out to the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group in the next 24 hours. Post exactly what you wrote here — confirmed use, weekly or more, constant lying and shutdown, rules not enforced, and feeling paralyzed by doubt. Ask how other parents have put first rules, rewards, and consequences in place when communication was this strained. Use that group as a place to vent, to reality-check whether you’re overreacting or underreacting, and to steady yourself so you can actually carry out the plan you’re building.

recommendations.title: Parent Emotional Regulation
recommendations.headline: Parent Emotional Regulation
recommendations.body: Right now you are near-daily exhausted, fearful, and losing sleep over your child’s safety. If you walk into conversations carrying all of that, your child sees the anger and panic, not your care. Before any serious talk, commit to a brief reset ritual: a few slow breaths, noticing your own tension, and deciding in advance what you will and will not say. If things heat up — yelling, door slamming, or you feel yourself about to say something you’ll regret — calmly say, “I’m pausing this. We’ll come back to it when we’re both calmer,” and step away. Write down what you want to communicate so you’re not winging it in the moment. Reach out to the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group and ask how others keep their voice steady when their teen denies and deflects. If you still find yourself shouting or freezing every time substance use comes up this week, the next step is to schedule regular brief check-ins with yourself and the group before any conversation with your child.

recommendations.title: Act on what you are seeing
recommendations.headline: Act on what you are seeing
recommendations.body: You have seen direct evidence of substance use, and you believe it’s happening weekly or more. This moves you from worrying to acting. In the next few days, outline one or two non-negotiable boundaries tied specifically to substance use, with clear rewards and clear consequences you know you can follow through on. For example: no driving or late-night hangouts until there is a period of clean tests and honest check-ins, paired with specific privileges your child can earn back. Use the Auxiliary Workshop "Intervening When Substance Use is Present: First Steps and Next Steps" to structure this: it will help you decide what happens if your child keeps using, lies, or refuses to talk. If substance use or strong suspicion continues this week after you’ve set and communicated those boundaries, the next step is to implement the planned consequence and immediately move toward outside evaluation for your child’s use.

recommendations.title: Get the adults aligned
recommendations.headline: Get the adults aligned
recommendations.body: You described the adults as pulling in opposite directions or not in contact. That makes any rule feel optional to your child. Your first move is a short, focused conversation (email, text, call, or in person) with the co-parent or co-guardian, if one exists, about three things only: (1) agreement that substance use is serious, (2) the few key rules about use, curfew, and access to high-risk settings, and (3) the rewards and consequences that will follow. Use the Essential Workshop "Building a Support Network" to think about which adults (relatives, coaches, others on the family side) can calmly back up these same messages. Bring what you agree on into a written list so it doesn’t change mid-argument. Reach out to the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group for scripts other parents have used when co-parents disagree. If you cannot get any alignment or response from other adults this week, the next step is to finalize your own clear plan in writing and share it with them anyway so there are no surprises later.

recommendations.title: Know what you are dealing with
recommendations.headline: Know what you are dealing with
recommendations.body: Because use is confirmed and the situation is serious, guessing what your child is using is not enough. A drug test you give is a fact-finding tool, not a punishment or threat. Plan for this in the back half of the week, after you and any other adults have agreed on what happens with the results. Tell your child plainly: “I’m giving a drug test so we both know what’s going on. The goal is safety, not catching you.” Use the Auxiliary Workshop "Drug Testing" to understand which tests to use, how often, and how to respond to different outcomes. Pair the test with clear rewards for clean results and clear consequences for refusal or positive results. If your child refuses a test or it shows ongoing use this week, the next step is to tighten previously agreed privileges and move toward an outside assessment for substance use and mental health.

recommendations.title: When every conversation turns into a fight
recommendations.headline: When every conversation turns into a fight
recommendations.body: You’re facing near-daily yelling and slammed doors, and you dread bringing up substance use because your child shuts down or blows up. That makes it impossible to deliver any plan. For the next week, your goal is smaller: short, calm interactions that don’t end in a fight. Use more statements and fewer questions that feel like interrogations. For example: “I’m concerned about what’s been going on with substances and I’m working on a plan to keep you safer. We’ll talk more about it on Thursday.” Use the Essential Workshop "Effective Communication: Building Trust and Engagement with Your Teen" to practice tone, timing, and listening skills that reduce escalation. Go into each talk expecting denial or blame, and prepare one calm line you will repeat instead of arguing. If every attempt at conversation still ends in shouting or total shutdown this week, the next step is to shorten the talks even more and deliver some of the key information in writing where your child can read it later.

recommendations.title: Make the rules mean something
recommendations.headline: Make the rules mean something
recommendations.body: Right now, rules are rarely enforced, and your child usually denies or blames others when there’s a problem. That teaches that limits are optional. Choose no more than three key rules related to safety: substance use, curfew, and communication about whereabouts. For each rule, set one specific reward for sticking to it and one specific consequence for breaking it — and commit to following through every time, calmly, without extra lectures. The Auxiliary Workshop "Behavioral Contracts – A Tool for Positive Change" can walk you through putting this into a written agreement your child signs. The Auxiliary Workshop "Setting Boundaries with Respect: Discipline Without Punishment" will help you enforce those limits without shaming or attacking. If your child continues to break these core rules and deny responsibility this week, the next step is to activate the next level of consequence already written into the agreement and keep it in place until they show consistent follow-through.

recommendations.title: When you are not getting straight answers
recommendations.headline: When you are not getting straight answers
recommendations.body: You reported constant secrecy, lying, and avoidance around substance questions. That means you need to gather facts in other ways. Quietly tighten your awareness of where your child goes, with whom, and what comes into the home. If you have serious concerns about safety or active use, you may need to search your child's room, backpack, or phone for substances or paraphernalia. Conduct any search of your child's room, backpack, or phone privately and without your child present. Leave the room as you found it and document anything relevant. The Auxiliary Workshop "How and When to Search a Room" will give you step-by-step guidance on doing this in a way that informs your plan instead of becoming a screaming match. If you find clear evidence of ongoing use this week, the next step is to bring that information into your already-planned boundaries and, if needed, move toward outside help for substance use.

recommendations.title: You cannot do this on empty
recommendations.headline: You cannot do this on empty
recommendations.body: You described feeling near-daily exhaustion, fear, and being overwhelmed. That level of strain will keep pulling you toward either exploding or avoiding. You need support not as a luxury, but so you can carry out the plan. In the next 24–48 hours, reach out to the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group and post honestly about your current situation — the frequent use, secrecy, conflict, and lack of school or professional support. Ask for very specific things: sample contracts, what consequences actually worked, how others handled unknown whereabouts. Protect one small part of each day (even 10–15 minutes) where you step away from the crisis and do something that steadies you: a walk, a call with a supportive friend, or just quiet time. If you are still feeling just as overwhelmed and paralyzed by doubt at the end of this week, the next step is to increase your contact with that group and consider adding an outside support person for yourself.

recommendations.title: What is underneath the behaviour
recommendations.headline: What is underneath the behaviour
recommendations.body: You’re seeing dramatic mood swings, withdrawal, and aggressive behaviour, and your child shuts down when stress or emotional pain is mentioned. Substance use may be your child’s way of numbing or coping. Alongside the rules around use, start naming that you see the emotional side too: “I notice your moods have been all over the place and you’ve been pulling away. I don’t know exactly what’s going on, but I’m not ignoring it.” The Auxiliary Workshop "Managing Stress and Pressure – Helping Your Teen Develop Healthy Coping Skills" will help you offer concrete alternatives to using — sleep routines, physical activity, small breaks, or other coping tools. If moods remain extreme or you see signs of self-harm, deep hopelessness, or dangerous behaviour this week, the next step is to seek professional help specifically for mood and substance use together. For guidance, consider posting questions in the Sustaining Recovery discussion group. In Admin Spaces, under Treatment Providers, you can find a listing of treatment providers & therapists who endorse and support the ASAP program.

recommendations.title: The people around your child
recommendations.headline: The people around your child
recommendations.body: You said your child spends almost all free time with peers you distrust, often in environments where substances may be present. That’s a major pathway into ongoing use. Rather than only forbidding certain friends, get curious about what your child gets from that group — belonging, excitement, escape. Ask short, non-judgmental questions when things are calmer, and state clear rules about where and when time with these peers is allowed, with matching rewards and consequences. The Auxiliary Workshop "Understanding and Navigating Peer Pressure" will help you understand how influence works so you can talk about it without turning it into an argument over specific friends. If your child continues to spend most free time with high-risk peers despite agreed rules this week, the next step is to tighten those limits further (for example, earlier curfews, supervised locations only) while you expand safer activities and connections.

recommendations.title: Bring the school in
recommendations.headline: Bring the school in
recommendations.body: You reported feeling completely alone, with no contact from school or community professionals. Yet school staff see your child for hours each day and may already notice changes in mood, peers, or performance. Within the next week, reach out to a key person at school — counselor, administrator, or teacher — and request a brief meeting or call focused on concern about substance use, behaviour changes, and safety, not just grades. The Auxiliary Workshop "Partnering with Schools for Your Child's Success" and the Essential Workshop "Building a Support Network" will help you prepare what to share and what to ask for (attendance info, behaviour observations, support options). If the school remains unresponsive or vague this week, the next step is to escalate your request (ask to speak with a higher-level staff member) and look for additional community supports to add eyes on your child.

recommendations.title: The phone and what is on it
recommendations.headline: The phone and what is on it
recommendations.body: You rarely know where your child is, and your child is often with peers you distrust. That likely means the phone and social media are a major supply line for substances and a source of pressure. You do not have to treat the phone as untouchable. Explain calmly that because of safety concerns and confirmed substance use, phone and social media will be supervised: app limits, no-phone times at night, and access contingent on behaviour. The Auxiliary Workshop "Understanding the Impact of Social Media on Substance Use and Mental Health" will give you ideas about specific risks to watch for and settings to change. If your child refuses any supervision of the phone or continues using it to arrange risky meetups this week, the next step is to temporarily reduce phone access according to the boundaries you already laid out, with clear steps to earn it back.

recommendations.title: Put the structure back
recommendations.headline: Put the structure back
recommendations.body: You described your child’s days as having very little routine and said you’re worried that your home doesn’t clearly discourage substance use. Without some rhythm to the day, rules and consequences float with nothing to attach to. This week, begin rebuilding a few anchors: consistent wake and sleep times, shared meals when possible, predictable expectations for school attendance or work, and clear norms that no substances are stored or used in the home by any family member. Physically remove or lock away alcohol, prescription medications, and anything else that could be misused. The Auxiliary Workshop "Creating a Healthy Home Environment – The Power of Structure and Routine" can help you design routines that fit your reality. If days are still chaotic, with your child coming and going unpredictably and substance access in the home not addressed by the end of this week, the next step is to tighten entry/exit expectations and supervision and enlist another adult to help you keep the home substance-free.

sections.title: What to avoid
items: Do not launch into a big confrontation about substance use while you are flooded with fear, anger, or exhaustion. In that state, it usually turns into shouting, threats, or desperate bargaining, which your child will either fight or ignore.

Do not keep adding more and more rules or harsher consequences without matching rewards and without actually following through. That teaches your child that you will back down if they yell or stonewall long enough.

Do not search your child's room, backpack, or phone confrontationally, in front of your child, or as a dramatic “gotcha.” Conduct any search of your child's room, backpack, or phone privately and without your child present. Leave the room as you found it and document anything relevant.

Do not rely only on taking away the phone, friends, or activities as your main response. If everything becomes punishment with no clear path to earn trust and privileges back, your child has no reason to choose better behaviour.

Do not stay completely isolated from other adults and from school. Trying to manage near-daily mood swings, secrecy, and suspected weekly use entirely on your own increases burnout and makes it more likely you’ll either give up or explode.

sections.title: Your first 72 hours
sections.body:
Day 1:
• Your only job today is to slow things down. Notice how often dread and panic show up when you think about substance use. When conflict starts, step away instead of engaging in yelling — say, “We’ll talk later,” and leave the room.
• Write down the top three concerns that keep you up at night (for example: safety when out, unknown substances, lying) and one or two rules you eventually want in place.
• In the evening, reach out to the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group, share this situation, and ask for examples of first boundaries that worked.

Day 2:
• Spend time on information and support, not yet on a big talk with your child.
• Watch the Auxiliary Workshop "Intervening When Substance Use is Present: First Steps and Next Steps" and take notes on what a clear first boundary and next step would look like for your family.
• Review basic information on common substances teens use in your area so you are not guessing.
• If there is a co-parent or co-guardian, contact them for a brief, focused alignment about substance rules, rewards, and consequences.

Day 3:
• Outline, in writing, the 2–3 key rules you’re going to communicate, along with the rewards and consequences you and any other adults agreed on.
• Choose a calm time to talk with your child (not right after a conflict or when either of you is rushing out the door).
• Keep the conversation short. State what you know (without debating details), that you’re acting because you care about safety, and the new boundaries: “Because of what I’ve seen with substances, here’s what will change…and here’s how you can earn things back.” Expect denial or anger; don’t argue about every point. Repeat your main message and end the talk if it escalates.

sections.title: Days 4 to 7
sections.body:
Over Days 4 to 7, you shift from talking about the plan to living it.

If your child denied everything or blamed others during the Day 3 conversation, hold the line you already set. You are not trying to win an argument; you are putting safety rules in place. Calmly apply the rewards and consequences you laid out, exactly as written, even if your child is angry or withdrawn.

In this window, prepare to give a drug test as a fact-finding step, guided by the Auxiliary Workshop "Drug Testing". Tell your child ahead of time that this will happen and how results connect to privileges. If your child refuses or a test shows ongoing use, follow through with the next level of consequence and begin seeking professional help for a fuller assessment of substance use and mood. For guidance, consider posting questions in the Sustaining Recovery discussion group. In Admin Spaces, under Treatment Providers, you can find a listing of treatment providers & therapists who endorse and support the ASAP program.

Also this week, make first contact with school using the Auxiliary Workshop "Partnering with Schools for Your Child's Success" as a guide. Keep posting in the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group about what’s actually happening — denials, escalations, small wins — and adjust the practical details of your plan, not the core boundaries.

workshops.whyThisFamily: You’re worried about being either too harsh or too lenient, and conflicts are intense. The Auxiliary Workshop "Setting Boundaries with Respect: Discipline Without Punishment" will show you how to hold firm lines on substance use and safety without shaming or escalating.

workshops.title: How and When to Search a Room
workshops.whyThisFamily: You described constant secrecy and lying about substances, so you may need to gather information without relying on your child’s word. The Auxiliary Workshop "How and When to Search a Room" will guide you in checking your child’s space and belongings in a quiet, non-dramatic way that informs your plan instead of becoming a new fight.

workshops.title: Managing Stress and Pressure – Helping Your Teen Develop Healthy Coping Skills
workshops.whyThisFamily: You’re seeing dramatic mood swings and withdrawal, and your child shuts down when stress is mentioned. The Auxiliary Workshop "Managing Stress and Pressure – Helping Your Teen Develop Healthy Coping Skills" will help you offer concrete coping tools so substances are not the only relief your child sees.

workshops.title: Understanding and Navigating Peer Pressure
workshops.whyThisFamily: Your child spends almost all free time with peers you distrust, often where substances may be present. The Auxiliary Workshop "Understanding and Navigating Peer Pressure" will help you understand how these friendships might be driving use and give you ways to talk about it without turning it into a battle over specific friends.

workshops.title: Partnering with Schools for Your Child's Success
workshops.whyThisFamily: You feel unsupported by school and have little idea what happens during your child’s day. The Auxiliary Workshop "Partnering with Schools for Your Child's Success" will help you approach school staff as allies, gather important information, and set up shared expectations around attendance, behaviour, and substance concerns.

workshops.whyThisFamily: You rarely know where your child is, and there is heavy time with high-risk peers, which likely runs through the phone. workshops.title: Creating a Healthy Home Environment – The Power of Structure and Routine
workshops.whyThisFamily: You described very little structure at home and worry that your environment sends mixed messages about substances. The Auxiliary Workshop "Creating a Healthy Home Environment – The Power of Structure and Routine" will help you rebuild daily routines and a clear no-use-at-home stance that every other part of this plan can rest on.

sections.title: Match the Intervention to the Risk
sections.body: The level of intervention should always match the level of risk. Too much intervention can be as counterproductive as too little. As concerns increase, your response should increase with them; as risk decreases, your response can adjust accordingly. The goal is not to use the strongest intervention available—it is to use the level of intervention that best matches what is actually happening with your child.

sections.title: Taking Care of Yourself
sections.body: Taking care of yourself is not a luxury—it’s a necessity. Whether you need some quiet time, a good workout, or the support of counseling, make space for what helps you stay grounded. When you care for yourself, you will be better able to show up strong, present, and healthy for you and your family.

sections.title: Where this can go
sections.body:
You’ve already done something many parents never do: you named the reality — confirmed use, frequent risk, constant conflict, and no plan — instead of looking away. That honesty is the starting point for change.

This next stretch will not be neat. Your child will almost certainly deny, deflect, or blow up when you bring in new boundaries. That doesn’t mean you are doing it wrong; it means the old pattern is being disrupted. Each time you hold a limit calmly instead of getting dragged into a fight, you are teaching that substances don’t run the household.

Remember: you and your child are on the same side of this, even when it doesn’t look like it. The opponent here is the pull of the substances and the chaos around them. Use the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group as a real-life bench of parents who know exactly what weekly use, lying, and slammed doors look like. You don’t have to carry every piece alone, and step by step, this can move from crisis management to a safer, more stable rhythm.

sections.title: Protecting the progress
sections.body:
Recovery is a journey—not a single event—and protecting the progress your child has already made is one of the most important responsibilities you have as a parent. While many adolescents go on to achieve lasting recovery, setbacks can occur. A setback does not erase the progress that has been made, and it does not have to become a return to the past.

Preparation is one of your greatest strengths. We encourage you to complete the Auxiliary Workshop "Protecting Recovery: Preventing Relapse and Responding to Setbacks." It will help you recognize early warning signs, respond calmly and effectively if challenges arise, and strengthen your family's plan to protect your child's recovery. We also encourage you to participate in the Protecting Recovery Discussion Group, where parents share experiences, encouragement, and practical insights while supporting one another through the ongoing journey of recovery.

Remember, the purpose of monitoring, supervision, conversations, and appropriate boundaries is not simply to discover what happened or when it happened—but to understand why. Identifying and addressing the underlying reasons for substance use gives your child the greatest opportunity for long-term recovery and a healthy, meaningful future.
